Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- As Hayden Henshaw was being rushed to the doctor's office after becoming ill, his father heard that his son's classmates had been struck with the deadly swine flu virus like the one sweeping through Mexico. Swine flu commonly affects pigs and occasionally infects people in contact with pigs. Patrick Henshaw called his wife immediately to have Hayden checked for it. Later, they received the bad news. Hayden had become the third confirmed case of swine flu at his Texas high school. It is a virus that has killed 68 people in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States. Health officials arrived at the Henshaws' house Friday and drew blood from the whole family, then told them to stay inside and away from the public, Henshaw told CNN. The whole family is quarantined indefinitely, according to CNN-affiliate KABB. Henshaw said his family was shocked when they got the news about their son. "Stunned. My wife was having a panic attack," Henshaw told the affiliate. U.S. health officials have expressed concern about U.S. cases of a swine flu virus that has similar characteristics to the fatal virus in Mexico. More than 1,000 people have fallen ill in Mexico City in a short period of time, U.S. health experts said. "This situation has been developing quickly," Richard Besser, acting director of the Atlanta, Georgia-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said Friday. "This is something we are worried about." Besser said all of the eight U.S. patients have recovered.  Watch for more on the U.S. cases » . New York health officials said Friday they were testing about 75 students at a school in New York City for swine flu after the students exhibited flu-like symptoms this week. A team of state health department doctors and staff went to the St. Francis Preparatory School in the borough of Queens on Thursday after the students reported cough, fever, sore throat, aches and pains. Test results are expected as early as Saturday. The new virus has genes from North American swine influenza, avian influenza, human influenza and a form of swine influenza normally found in Asia and Europe, said Nancy Cox, chief of the CDC's Influenza Division. Swine flu is caused by a virus similar to a type of flu virus that infects people every year but is a strain typically found only in pigs -- or in people who have direct contact with pigs. There have, however, been cases of person-to-person transmission of swine flu, the CDC said. CNN's David Alsup contributed to this report.

A Texas high school student has become the third confirmed case of swine flu in the United States, health officials said, as federal authorities monitor a widening outbreak that has killed people in Mexico and raised concerns about possible spread in American schools.

The student, identified as **Hayden Henshaw**, attends high school in Texas and is recovering, officials said. As a precaution, Henshaw’s family has been asked to remain under quarantine while health workers track anyone who may have had close contact with him.

In Mexico, authorities have reported multiple deaths suspected to be linked to the outbreak, prompting school closures and public health warnings in parts of the country. U.S. officials said they are coordinating with Mexican health authorities and the World Health Organization to determine whether cases in both countries are connected.

Meanwhile, health officials in **New York City** are investigating possible swine flu cases at a school after a number of students reported flu-like symptoms. Samples from the students were being tested to determine whether they match the same strain confirmed in Texas and elsewhere.

Public health officials urged calm but advised people to take standard flu precautions: wash hands frequently, cover coughs and sneezes, stay home when sick, and seek medical advice if symptoms worsen.

The CDC said it is continuing surveillance nationwide and will provide updates as more laboratory results become available.

# U.S. swine flu cases rise as officials trace new virus strain

**By [Staff Writer]**  
**CNN.com**  
**April 2009**

ATLANTA, Georgia — Federal health officials said Sunday they are tracking a growing number of swine flu cases in the United States as investigators try to determine how a new strain of influenza spread from scattered patients in California and Texas to a wider public health concern.

Among the early U.S. cases was **Hayden Henshaw**, a young boy from San Diego County, California, whose diagnosis helped alert doctors and public health officials to an unusual form of influenza not typically seen in humans.

Hayden’s illness began with flu-like symptoms — fever, coughing and fatigue — that at first appeared similar to the seasonal flu cases physicians see every year. But laboratory testing later showed that he had been infected with a previously unrecognized strain of swine-origin influenza A, health officials said.

After the diagnosis, the **Henshaw family was asked to remain at home under quarantine-like precautions** while local and federal health officials monitored them for symptoms and tried to determine whether the virus had spread to relatives, classmates or others in the community. Family members were advised to limit contact with others, watch for fever or respiratory symptoms and cooperate with county health workers as they investigated the case.

Health officials said Hayden recovered, and his case did not appear to be severe. But the unusual nature of the virus — and the fact that other cases soon appeared in different locations — prompted a broader investigation by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

## CDC: Virus contains genetic material from several flu strains

Scientists at the **CDC** said genetic analysis of the virus showed that it was a **new swine flu strain**, containing a combination of genetic material from influenza viruses previously found in pigs, birds and humans.

The strain is commonly described as a swine-origin influenza A H1N1 virus. CDC officials said the virus was notable because it appeared to include gene segments from North American swine flu viruses as well as Eurasian swine flu viruses — a combination not previously identified in people in the United States.

“This is a novel influenza virus,” CDC officials said, adding that because humans would likely have little pre-existing immunity to it, the agency was treating the situation with heightened concern.

The CDC said it was working with state health departments, the World Health Organization and officials in Mexico and Canada to compare virus samples, track transmission and determine whether the outbreak could be contained.

## U.S. cases confirmed in multiple states

By late April 2009, confirmed U.S. cases had been reported in several states, including **California, Texas, Kansas, New York and Ohio**, according to public health officials. Most U.S. patients had experienced mild illness and recovered, but authorities warned that the situation could change quickly as more testing was completed.

At least some U.S. cases were not linked to direct contact with pigs, suggesting that the virus was spreading from person to person. That finding raised concern among public health experts because seasonal influenza spreads easily through coughing, sneezing and close contact.

Officials urged people with flu symptoms to stay home from school or work, cover coughs and sneezes, wash hands frequently and seek medical attention if symptoms worsened.

## Mexico reports far larger outbreak

The concern in the United States was heightened by reports from **Mexico**, where authorities were investigating a much larger outbreak of severe respiratory illness.

Mexican officials reported **more than 1,000 suspected cases** and dozens of deaths believed to be possibly linked to the new flu strain. At the time, laboratory confirmation was still under way, and officials cautioned that not all suspected cases would necessarily prove to be swine flu.

Mexico City took extraordinary measures to slow the spread of illness, closing schools, canceling public events and advising residents to avoid large gatherings. Images from the capital showed people wearing surgical masks in public places as health workers screened patients for symptoms.

The World Health Organization said it was monitoring the outbreak closely and coordinating with national governments. Officials said the combination of confirmed U.S. cases and severe illnesses in Mexico warranted urgent international attention.

## Family’s case becomes part of larger investigation

For the Henshaw family, what began as one child’s illness quickly became part of a national epidemiological investigation.

Local health officials interviewed the family about Hayden’s recent activities, possible exposures and close contacts. Investigators sought to determine whether he had traveled, visited farms, been near pigs or had contact with anyone who had recently been ill.

Health officials said such interviews are standard during an outbreak investigation and are essential for determining how a new virus is spreading.

While the family’s quarantine precautions were disruptive, public health experts said such steps can help reduce the chance of transmission while investigators assess risk.

## Officials urge caution, not panic

The CDC said it was preparing guidance for doctors, hospitals and state health agencies. Antiviral medications such as oseltamivir and zanamivir were expected to be effective against the virus, officials said, though they emphasized that treatment decisions should be made by medical professionals.

Federal officials said they were also examining whether existing flu vaccine stockpiles would provide any protection. Early indications suggested that the seasonal flu vaccine was unlikely to offer strong protection against the newly identified strain.

Health authorities emphasized that people should not panic but should take basic precautions.

“This is a rapidly evolving situation,” officials said. “We expect to find more cases as surveillance expands.”

The CDC said additional laboratory testing and genetic sequencing would continue as investigators worked to determine how widespread the virus was, how severe the illness could become and whether additional public health measures would be needed.

**CNN contributor credit:** CNN’s medical and health unit, along with local affiliates in California, contributed to this report.
